notes.meaning: The long family lists in the earlier chapters close here. They came from Israel's official public records, not from the Bible books we call Kings. Then comes a sad line: Judah was taken away to Babylon because the people were unfaithful to God. Matthew Henry says this judgment should be remembered as a warning, and that when trouble comes we can honestly say, "it was for my sin."

After the exile in Babylon, the first people came home and moved back onto their own family land. There were four groups. They were ordinary Israelites, priests, Levites (the tribe set apart to help the priests), and temple servants. The temple servants were workers "given" to help at God's house, possibly coming from the Gibeonites of Joshua's day. Wesley notes that the old shared name "Israelites" is used again, a sign that the split between the two kingdoms was now gone.

Most of the people in Jerusalem came from Judah and Benjamin. But some came from Ephraim and Manasseh, tribes of the old northern kingdom. Many of them had fled south to Judah long before and later shared Judah's exile and return. Matthew Henry sees here the start of God's promise that Judah and Israel would be gathered together again as one people (Hosea 1:11).

Uthai is the first leader from Judah. His family went back to Perez, one of Judah's sons. This list is much like the one in Nehemiah 11, but some names differ. Wesley explains that people often had more than one name, and that Nehemiah's list also includes people who came back later.
Asaiah led the second family from Judah. "Shilonites" probably does not mean people from the town of Shiloh. It most likely means descendants of Shelah, another of Judah's sons.
Jeuel led the third family from Judah, the descendants of Zerah. The 690 relatives seem to count the family heads from all three of Judah's families, Perez, Shelah, and Zerah, taken together.

Next come four leaders from the tribe of Benjamin, with 956 relatives. Nehemiah gives a slightly different number. Wesley thinks the lists counted at different times or in different ways. Matthew Henry notes that many people stayed behind in Babylon. Those whose hearts God stirred to go home deserve to be remembered with honor.

Now the priests are listed. Jedaiah, Jehoiarib, and Jachin are names of priestly family groups that took turns serving. Matthew Henry praises the priests for coming back with the first group. He asks, who should lead in a good work if not the Lord's ministers?

Azariah is called the chief official of God's temple. Most of these commentators say he was not the high priest himself. He was the next in charge, a kind of deputy who helped run the temple. Matthew Henry says God's house needs leaders, not to make new laws, but to see that God's laws are kept.

Two more priestly leaders are named, Adaiah and Maasai, from the priestly groups of Malchijah and Immer. With them were 1,760 relatives. The words "able men" really mean "mighty men of valor," like brave soldiers. Serving God took courage and strength. The priests had to guard holy things and keep out what was unclean, even when people pushed back.

Now the Levites are listed. Some came from the family of Merari. Others came from Asaph and Jeduthun, the great families of temple singers, so these men were probably music leaders. Berechiah's family lived in villages near Netophah, close to Bethlehem. Matthew Henry suggests some lived outside the city because there was not yet room for them in Jerusalem.

The gatekeepers guarded the gates of God's house so that nothing and no one unclean could come in. Four chiefs each led a team for one side of the temple, with Shallum as head. He kept the King's Gate on the east, the entrance the king used to go into the temple. "The camp of the Levites" is an old phrase. It recalls the wilderness days, when the Levites camped around the tabernacle.

Shallum came from the family of Korah. He and his relatives guarded the doorways of God's house, just as their ancestors had guarded the tabernacle's entrance in the wilderness. Their job was to keep out anyone not allowed into the holy places. Wesley says everything was being put back in its first good order. Matthew Henry notes that the work looked lowly. Yet the psalmist would rather be a doorkeeper in God's house than live with the wicked (Psalm 84:10).

Long before, Phinehas son of Eleazar had been in charge of the gatekeepers. Keil & Delitzsch place this in Joshua's time, while Phinehas's father was high priest. Matthew Henry thought it might be a lesser-known Levite with the same name. An old Aramaic paraphrase reads, "the Word of the Lord was his helper." The note reminded later gatekeepers that God would be with them too.

Zechariah guarded the door of the Tent of Meeting, the tent where God met with his people, in King David's time. Before the temple was built, God's people worshiped at this simple, movable tent. Wesley draws a lesson from this. If we cannot yet have a temple, we should be thankful for a tent and use it well. God's work should never be left undone for lack of a building.

There were 212 gatekeepers. They lived in nearby villages and came to Jerusalem in turns, about a week at a time. Samuel the seer, an old word for prophet, began to plan this order of service. David later finished it. They were given these "positions of trust" because they had proved themselves faithful.
